claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with a uniform, ductile microstructure.
Service-relevant high-magnitude mechanical loading creates a high density of mobile dislocations.
A high density of mobile dislocations locally destabilizes the initially homogeneous solid solution.
Dislocation accumulation drives localized atomic reordering and compositional segregation.
Localized segregation nucleates nanoscale brittle precipitates preferentially at dislocation pile-ups.
Nanoscale brittle precipitates at dislocation pile-ups act as crack-initiation sites.
The precipitates reduce overall fracture toughness.
Identical samples will be compared after one set receives high-stress or high-strain-rate tensile or cyclic loading and the other remains unloaded.
Composition and processing history will be controlled so that mechanical loading is the principal difference between the sample sets.
Mechanical loading produces evolving dislocation structures during deformation.
Lattice distortions inherent to high-entropy alloys promote load-induced localized atomic reordering.
Brittle precipitates interfere with plastic energy absorption and cause a transition from ductile to brittle fracture.
The loaded sample will have lower crack-initiation or fracture toughness than the unloaded baseline.
The loaded sample's fracture surface will be dominated by cleavage rather than ductile dimples.
TEM or comparable microscopy will reveal localized nanoscale precipitates at former dislocation pile-up sites in the loaded sample.
The unloaded as-cast baseline retains a homogeneous microstructure and ductile fracture characteristics.
The governing behavior is expected near demanding service limits involving high stress or strain rate at the service temperature.
The critical strain or stress for phase instability and the magnitude of toughness loss may depend on alloy composition and processing history.
Failure to observe both a significant toughness reduction and localized brittle precipitates in loaded samples would falsify the hypothesis.
